To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
swabbing a touch surface in a volume crime case has a 40.7% chance of leading to a positive result (DNA profile) and a 20.6% chance of leading a hit in the database.

swabs targeting a single surface are more successful than swabs targeting multiple surfaces, swabs taken on a single object are more successful than those taken on multiple objects, swabs targeting a biological fluid are more successful than touch surface swabs, and swabs taken in the laboratory are more successful than scene swabs.
swabbing a single surface is better than swabbing different ones, and that swabbing on some objects is better than swabs on others.

swabbing door and window handles, and other surfaces that have been touched, is a worthwhile effort, whereas
swabs taken on touch surfaces in operational situations have the best chance to yield a DNA profile.

the results of the study can be used by the forensic scientists to inform the crime scene investigators about what should be swabbed and what not.
it provides the first operational study of DNA swabs success rates in a police department, which could be used to inform an evidence-based triage and crime scene investigation approach.

The main takeaway from our work is that
, when possible, swabs should be targeted on a single surface and that the choice of the surface should be guided by the success rate observed in the past for that particular surface.
the success rate of a DNA swab is not only influenced by its quality (i.e., the number of cells deposited by the target specimen) but also by the situation where it was taken.
the success rate of a DNA swab is not random and that some criteria can be used to predict the chance that the DNA analysis of a given swab will result in a positive outcome.
